what_its_for: Rufinamide is a seizure medicine (antiepileptic drug) used to help control seizures in people with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, a severe form of epilepsy that causes many different types of seizures. It helps reduce how often and how severe your seizures are.
how_to_take: Take rufinamide by mouth WITH food — this is very important because food helps your body absorb the medicine better and reduces stomach upset. Swallow the tablets whole or you may crush them and mix with water if you have trouble swallowing. If you take an oral suspension (liquid), shake the bottle well before each use and use the measuring device provided — never use a regular kitchen spoon. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribed.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time. The dose is based on your weight and other medicines you take. Adults usually take it twice a day (every 12 hours), morning and evening. Children also take it twice daily, with doses based on body weight. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first — stopping suddenly can cause more seizures.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to the time for your next dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store rufinamide tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them in a dry place away from moisture and heat — do not store in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. For the oral liquid suspension, store at room temperature and use within 90 days of opening — throw away any unused liquid after 90 days. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking rufinamide because it can increase dizziness and drowsiness and raise your risk of serious side effects. Be careful driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything requiring alertness until you know how this medicine affects you — it can cause dizziness and sleepiness. Avoid stopping this medicine suddenly without your doctor's guidance. Tell all your doctors and dentists that you take this medicine before any procedure or surgery.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: new or worsening depression, anxiety, unusual mood changes, or thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide; a serious skin rash, especially one with blistering, peeling, or sores in your mouth (possible sign of a rare but dangerous reaction called Stevens-Johnson Syndrome); high fever, swollen lymph nodes, or yellowing of the skin or eyes; shortness of breath, fast or irregular heartbeat; severe dizziness or loss of coordination; or if your seizures get worse or you have a new type of seizure. Also contact your doctor if you become pregnant while taking this medicine.
when_it_works: Rufinamide does not work right away. Your doctor will gradually increase your dose over several weeks to find the right amount for you. Most people begin to notice fewer or less severe seizures within a few weeks to a couple of months after reaching their target dose. Keep taking it every day even if you feel well — do not stop just because your seizures seem controlled.
special_populations: Children: Rufinamide is approved for children 1 year and older (or 4 years and older depending on your country). Doses are based on the child's weight. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Rufinamide may harm an unborn baby, but uncontrolled seizures also carry serious risks — your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Women of childbearing age should discuss contraception with their doctor, as rufinamide may make hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings) less effective. Breastfeeding: It is not known if rufinamide passes into breast milk — talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and should use caution to prevent falls.
